claims.text: Rapid quenching followed by controlled low-temperature annealing will produce nanoscale precipitates in a magnetic high-entropy alloy.
The nanoscale precipitates will act as magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
Pinning by the precipitates will increase the energy barrier to domain-wall motion.
Increasing the energy barrier to domain-wall motion will increase the coercive field.
The quenched and annealed alloy will have a higher coercive field than the untreated homogeneous baseline.
With an optimal precipitate size and distribution, the coercive-field increase will be significant relative to measurement uncertainty.
An inert atmosphere is required to prevent oxidation during processing.
Annealing temperature and duration can be adjusted to favor nanoscale precipitation while avoiding excessive coarsening.
The coercivity-enhancing effect requires precipitates in an optimal nanoscale size range.
Precipitates that are too coarse may fail to increase the coercive field.
If the alloy composition does not favor precipitate formation under the stated treatment, the intervention may not increase coercivity.
The magnitude of coercivity enhancement depends on precipitate size, precipitate density, and alloy composition.
